'''Miriam Daniel Mann''' (1907–1967) was one of the first Black [[computer (occupation)|female computers]] for the [[National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics]] (NACA).

==Biography==
Mann was born in 1907, in Covington, Georgia.<ref name="Macalester College">{{cite web |title=Biography of Miriam D. Mann · Human Computers at NASA |url=https://omeka.macalester.edu/humancomputerproject/items/show/34 |website=Macalester College |access-date=15 April 2022}}</ref> She attended [[Talladega College]]. She was married to Bill Mann,<ref name="Washington Post"/> with whom she had three children.<ref name="BBC News"/> In 1943, in the wake of labor shortages caused by [[World War II]], Mann responded to a recruitment drive for Black female mathematicians by the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA).<ref name="BBC News">{{cite web |title=Hidden Figures: How Nasa hired its first black women 'computers' |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/magazine-39003904 |website=BBC News |access-date=16 April 2022 |date=18 February 2017}}</ref> She subsequently attended a 10-week training course at [[Hampton Institute]] and was accepted for a position as a "human computer".<ref name="Washington Post"/><ref name="Biography">{{cite web |last1=Collazo |first1=Julie Schwietert |title=NASA's Hidden Figures: The Unsung Women You Need to Know |url=https://www.biography.com/news/hidden-figures-movie-real-women |website=Biography |access-date=16 April 2022 |language=en-us}}</ref> At the time she was hired the state of Virginia was [[Racial segregation in the United States|segregated]], as was the NACA campus at [[Langley Air Force Base|Langley]], Virginia. Mann repeatedly removed the "COLORED COMPUTERS" sign segregating the cafeteria. The sign was replaced each time until Mann removed it a final time and it was never replaced.<ref name="Shortform Books">{{cite web |last1=Cabral |first1=Carrie |title=Miriam Mann and the Daily Protests That Changed NASA |url=https://www.shortform.com/blog/miriam-mann-hidden-figures/ |website=Shortform Books |access-date=16 April 2022 |date=1 June 2020}}</ref>

Mann worked for NACA (which became [[NASA]] in 1958) until her retirement in 1966.<ref name="Washington Post">{{cite web |last1=Sichynsky |first1=Tanya |title=How World War II opened the door for one of the first black women at NASA |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/arts-and-entertainment/wp/2016/09/19/how-world-war-ii-opened-the-door-for-one-of-the-first-black-women-at-nasa/ |website=Washington Post |access-date=16 April 2022}}</ref> She died in 1967.<ref name="Macalester College"/>

In 2017 Mann's granddaughter [[Duchess Harris]] co-authored a book with Sue Bradford Edwards entitled ''Hidden Human Computers: The Black Women of NASA''.<ref name="ABDO">{{cite web |title=Hidden Human Computers: The Black Women of NASA |url=https://abdobooks.com/shop/show/9454 |website=ABDO |access-date=16 April 2022}}</ref> In 2018 the Virginia Capitol Foundation announced that Mann's name would be on the [[Virginia Women's Monument]]'s glass Wall of Honor.<ref name="Virginia Women's Monument Commission">{{cite web |title=Wall of Honor |url=http://womensmonumentcom.virginia.gov/wallofhonornames.html |website=Virginia Women's Monument Commission |access-date=16 April 2022}}</ref>
